commands.desc: generate a starter CLAUDE.md for this repo

steps.t: reading the repo — structure, conventions, tooling …
created CLAUDE.md
# CLAUDE.md
stack: Next.js 15, TypeScript, Tailwind, Cloudflare Workers
test: npm test · build: npm run cf:build
never fabricate an API — say "I don't know" honestly
CLAUDE.md loads every session — teach Claude your repo once, it remembers

commands.desc: edit CLAUDE.md, manage auto-memory

steps.t: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md   — your personal rules, every project
./CLAUDE.md           — this repo's rules, shared with your team
./CLAUDE.local.md     — your own notes for this repo, gitignored
auto-memory: Claude writes its OWN notes as it learns — no manual effort
a fix Claude got right once, a build quirk, a preference you stated — remembered
CLAUDE.md is what YOU write; auto-memory is what Claude writes for itself
why it matters

The power here is compounding: every correction you'd otherwise repeat, every build quirk Claude would otherwise re-discover, gets written down once and never re-explained. A team that checks CLAUDE.md into git gives every new session — and every teammate — the same accumulated context from day one.

commands.desc: connect Claude to your other tools

steps.t: MCP — Model Context Protocol, an open standard for AI-tool connections
an MCP server gives Claude Code access to a real tool — Jira, GitHub, Postgres, Figma
connect once, then just ask in plain language — no more copy-pasting data into chat
"Add the feature from JIRA-4521 and open a PR on GitHub" — MCP makes this literal
hundreds of MCP servers exist already — connect one before building your own
why it matters

Before MCP, giving Claude context meant copy-pasting it in. After connecting a server once, you ask in plain language and Claude reaches the real system directly — hundreds of servers already exist for common tools, so the first move is almost always to connect one rather than build one.

commands.desc: decide what Claude may do without asking

steps.t: permission rules — allow, ask, or deny, per tool
Claude uses this tool without stopping to ask
Claude always prompts you first, every time
the tool is refused — or removed from context entirely
"Bash(npm test *)" allowed · "Bash(git push *)" always asks
deny always wins — a broader deny rule beats a narrower allow rule
rules can be checked into git — a whole team inherits the same guardrails
why it matters

This is what makes autonomy safe to grant. Once you trust `npm test` and reading any file, Claude stops interrupting you for them — but `git push` still asks, and `.env` is unreadable no matter what. Rules committed to git mean an entire team inherits the same guardrails instead of each developer re-approving the same commands one at a time.

commands.desc: your own commands, taught once

steps.t: a skill is a folder with a SKILL.md — Claude adds it to its toolkit
write it once for a task you keep re-explaining: a deploy checklist, a review procedure
invoke it directly with /your-skill-name, or Claude reaches for it automatically
only loads into context when actually used — unlike CLAUDE.md, it costs nothing idle
bundled — troubleshoots the current session
bundled — finds bugs + cleanups in your diff
.claude/commands/deploy.md and .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md both create /deploy
why it matters

Skills only load into context when actually used — unlike CLAUDE.md, a library of 50 skills costs nothing until one is needed. You can write down every procedure you have (deploys, migrations, incident response) without any of it competing for context space on an unrelated task. They're shareable too — package one into a plugin and an entire org inherits the same procedure.

commands.desc: design before you build

steps.t: plan mode: Claude reads and explores, but won't edit your source files yet
use it before a large or risky change — get a reviewable plan first
you approve the plan, THEN Claude implements it
planning up front costs a few minutes; an unplanned rewrite can cost hours
why it matters

The value scales with the size of the change: a five-minute plan review catches a wrong assumption before it becomes two hours of code built on it. It turns "big scary refactor" into "a plan I can read, edit, and approve" — much easier to trust than a diff that appears all at once.

commands.desc: switch model, save as your default

steps.t: select the model you pair with:
Fable 5           — most intelligent, generally available
Sonnet 5          — fast, strong daily driver
Opus 4.8          — deep reasoning, harder problems
Haiku 4.5         — fastest, cheapest
/model swaps mid-task — your context and history survive the swap

commands.desc: trade speed for depth of reasoning

steps.t: levels: low · medium · high · xhigh · max
low/medium — quick, cheap answers for small mechanical tasks
high/xhigh — more thorough reasoning for genuinely hard problems
takes effect immediately, without waiting for the current response to finish

commands.desc: visualize what is filling your context window

steps.t: a colored grid — CLAUDE.md, tool results, conversation history, each a block
shows optimization suggestions for context-heavy tools and memory bloat
check this before a long session gets sluggish, not after

commands.desc: summarize the conversation to free context

steps.t: summarizing the conversation …
context: 84% -> 12%
compact often on long sessions — a clear context window reasons better

commands.desc: ask a quick side question, off the record

steps.t: /btw what does this regex actually match?
answers without adding to the conversation history — no context cost
good for a curiosity question mid-task that isn't part of the actual work

commands.desc: delegate side-tasks to a subagent

steps.t: a subagent runs in its own context window, then reports back a summary
use one when a side task would flood your main chat with logs or file contents
give it a narrow tool set and a focused system prompt — specialise it
route cheap side-work to a faster, cheaper model to control cost
bundled — broad read-only codebase search
bundled — designs an implementation plan
ask Claude to "create a subagent for X" — it writes the .claude/agents/ file for you
why it matters

This is the difference between a session that degrades after an hour of exploration and one that stays sharp for a full day of work: side research, log-diving, and file-trawling happen somewhere else, and only the conclusion comes back. Route a subagent to a cheaper, faster model for mechanical work, and run many in parallel — turning one conversation into a small team.

commands.desc: decompose a large change across parallel worktrees

steps.t: researching the codebase, decomposing the work …
presents a plan first — approve before anything runs
each unit gets its own background subagent, in its own git worktree
each subagent implements, tests, and opens its own pull request
example: "/batch migrate src/ from Solid to React" — a whole migration, unattended
why it matters

This is how you stop being the bottleneck on your own codebase. A migration touching 30 files doesn't have to happen one file at a time in one conversation — it can fan out into 30 isolated subagents, each testing and opening its own PR, while you review the results instead of writing them.

commands.desc: detach a session to keep running unattended

steps.t: frees your terminal — the session keeps working in the background
monitor it with claude agents; reattach any time
alias: /bg — good for a long task you don't need to watch line by line

commands.desc: spawn a background copy without switching away

steps.t: a forked subagent inherits the full conversation, works on a side directive
you keep going in the main conversation; the fork's result returns when done
compare: /branch switches YOU into a copy; /fork sends the copy off on its own

commands.desc: see exactly what changed

steps.t: an interactive diff viewer — uncommitted changes and per-turn diffs
left/right arrows switch between the full diff and individual Claude turns
reviewing turn-by-turn shows you exactly which change did what

commands.desc: review the current diff for bugs + cleanups

steps.t: reading the working tree …
auth.ts — clean · one responsibility, well-named
handler.ts:14 — function does 6 unrelated things, consider splitting
schema.json — no vulnerable dependency versions
pass --fix to apply the findings, --comment to post them on a GitHub PR
/code-review ultra runs a deep multi-agent review in the cloud

commands.desc: check the diff for vulnerabilities

steps.t: scanning pending changes for security issues …
api/upload.ts:22 — file path built from user input, unvalidated
looks for injection, auth issues, and data exposure specifically
run this on anything touching auth, file paths, or user input before merging

commands.desc: cleanup-only review, applies fixes directly

steps.t: four review agents run in parallel: reuse, simplification, efficiency, abstraction level
doesn't hunt for bugs — that's /code-review's job
applies the cleanup fixes directly, no separate approval step
run /code-review first for correctness, /simplify after for polish

commands.desc: start fresh, keeping project memory

steps.t: fresh start — ਸਹਿਜ (clean scrollback, clear mind)
the previous conversation stays available in /resume
CLAUDE.md and auto-memory carry over — you're not starting from zero
use /compact instead if you want to keep the SAME conversation, just lighter

commands.desc: return to a past conversation

steps.t: opens a picker of past sessions, or resume by name / ID directly
background sessions show up marked "bg" in the picker
alias: /continue

commands.desc: try a different direction without losing your place

steps.t: creates a branch of the CURRENT conversation, right where you are
switches you into the branch; the original stays intact
return to the original any time with /resume
good for "what if I tried it this other way" without losing the first attempt

commands.desc: label the current session

steps.t: renames the session and shows the name on the prompt bar
without a name, auto-generates one from the conversation so far
makes a long-running session easy to find later in /resume

commands.desc: roll code + conversation back to a checkpoint

steps.t: rewinds code AND conversation together, to a point you pick
or just summarize from a selected message onward
aliases: /checkpoint, /undo — the safety net for a change that went wrong
why it matters

It turns every risky change into a reversible one. You don't need to be certain before you let Claude try something — if the direction is wrong, you roll back to before it started and try again, at the cost of a few minutes instead of a `git reset` archaeology session.

steps.t: checking installation and settings …
a plugin failed to load — stale cache detected
press f to have Claude fix any reported issue directly
first stop when something about Claude Code itself seems broken

describe the issue and Claude reads the session debug log to investigate
a bundled skill — for THIS session's behavior, not the install itself (use /doctor for that)
